newsitem.title: JAPAN: BOJ governor says backs panel's reform proposals.
newsitem.headline: BOJ governor says backs panel's reform proposals.

text.p: Bank of Japan Governor Yasuo Matsushita said on Tuesday that he strongly hopes reforms of the central bank are carried out based on proposals submitted by an advisory panel to the prime minister earlier in the day.

"The Bank of Japan strongly hopes that the review of various systems, including the law governing the BOJ, will be quickly realised, based on the basic policy outlined in the panel's report," Matsushita said.

The panel advising Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto earlier issued proposals to enhance the central bank's independence and urged the bank to make its policy making system more transparent. The group's proposals will be considered by government panels before being formally adopted by the government.
The BOJ said in a statement that it would also consider ways to reform its organisation in parallel with the government review and hoped to conclude it by next spring.
Matsushita said the central bank would consider holding regular policy-board meetings to decide policy on the discount rate and money market operations.
It would also consider disclosing the minutes of the board meetings as a way to boost transparency, he said.
Matsushita said the bank would study ways to improve the settlement system, including the possible introduction of real-time settlements, after discussions with market participants.

He said other things to consider were the BOJ's inspections of financial institutions, and using the Internet to dispatch information on the BOJ's monetary policy management. The BOJ would review its inspections so that they would not cover the same ground as government inspections, he said.

The supervisory right of the Ministry of Finance (MOF) over the BOJ would be discussed later and further studies of the relationship between the bank and the government would have to be carried out, he said.
Asked if the BOJ thought that allowing government representatives at BOJ policy board meetings would undermine the central bank's independence, Matsushita said:

"The board meetings must not hurt the BOJ's independence. I have no objection to the direction outlined by the study group toward strengthening the system of the policy board. Specifics such as who become board members will be studied further."

Commenting on a proposal that the government should make decisions on foreign exchange intervention policy, Matsushita said he did not see the immediate need to change the current methods of intervention.
At present the BOJ intervenes in the currency market on behalf of the government.

Commenting on a panel proposal that government representatives be allowed to attend policy-board meetings and to submit proposals, Matsushita said this was not necessarily out of step with global practice and was the system in Germany and some other European countries.
He said that allowing the government to voice its opinion in an official setting would help increase transparency in the BOJ's policy-making process.
"I don't think the government will persistently use such a right to put pressure on the Bank of Japan," he said.
